story_title: The Element With Too Many Weights
tagline: Keep element identity fixed while neutron counts and isotope abundance change.

guide.name: Dr. Mina Cho
guide.visual: white lab coat, black clipboard, and a brass proton counter
guide.story_job: Mina keeps proton count, neutron count, isotope mass, and abundance physically separated.

premise: A shipment of atoms has arrived with one element label but several measured masses.
mission: Sort atoms by proton and neutron count, then reconstruct the weighted average that appears on the periodic table.
finale: The records hall accepts several isotopes under one element identity and prints one weighted average atomic mass.
route_orientation: Enter the sorting gate, then continue straight to the weighted balance console.

story_paragraphs: The **Atomic Records Hall** opens at a sorting gate with three fixed lanes. On your left, every incoming atom receives the same brass proton badge. In the center, clear nucleus models arrive on a conveyor. On the right, a record board waits for a label. Dr. Mina Cho locks the proton counter so it cannot change while the first two nuclei move under the light.

The two nuclei carry the same number of protons, so Mina keeps the element name unchanged. One nucleus carries extra neutron crates. The other carries fewer. Only after you can see the fixed proton count and the changing neutron count does she place the word **isotope** on the record board. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons.

Mina taps the permanent proton badge and writes **atomic number** beside it. Atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus and identifies the element. Then she turns to a separate headcount display that adds protons and neutrons for one nucleus. That total is the **mass number**. The two quantities sit on different sides of the gate so they cannot be merged.

story_beats.science: Atoms of the same element can differ in neutron count.
story_beats.hint: Same proton badge, different neutron crates.

story_beats.science: Atomic number equals the number of protons and identifies the element.
Mass number equals protons plus neutrons for one isotope.

scenes.title: The periodic-table value is a weighted average
scenes.scene_kicker: Let isotope abundance determine how strongly each isotope pulls on the final average.
scenes.location_description: A calculation desk with isotope masses on the left, fractional abundances in the center, and a summing balance on the right.

scene_layout.orientation: Face the balance console. Isotope masses stay on the left, fractional abundances stay in the center, and the summed weighted value appears on the right.

zones.label: Isotope mass cards
zones.description: Each card gives the mass for one isotope.

zones.label: Abundance dials
zones.description: Each dial converts percentage abundance to a fraction.

zones.label: Weighted sum balance
zones.description: The console multiplies each isotope mass by its fractional abundance and adds the contributions.

cast.name: Dr. Mina Cho
cast.visual: black clipboard beside the balance console
cast.job: Makes each multiplication visible before the sum appears.

cast.name: Weighted sum balance
cast.visual: two balance arms feeding a single digital total

story_paragraphs: A short corridor ends at a balance console. The left tray holds isotope-mass cards. The middle panel holds abundance dials. The right display is blank. Mina places a 10.0 amu card beside a 20.0% dial and an 11.0 amu card beside an 80.0% dial. The console refuses to average 10 and 11 directly.

She turns each percentage into a fraction, multiplies each isotope mass by its own fractional abundance, and sends both products to the final display. Only then does the console show 10.8 amu. Mina labels the process **average atomic mass**. Average atomic mass is the weighted average of the naturally occurring isotope masses using their fractional abundances.

The equation remains lit above the scale as Σ(isotopic mass × fractional abundance). A rare isotope contributes less to the final value than a common isotope. The balance therefore records both mass and abundance, which is why a periodic-table atomic mass need not match the mass number of any single isotope.

story_beats.science: Average atomic mass is a weighted average based on isotope mass and fractional abundance.

scenes.checkpoint_prompt: What quantity is calculated by summing each isotope mass multiplied by its fractional abundance?
scenes.checkpoint_hint: Picture the Σmf balance at the right side of the desk.
